name: LearnPack Pedagogical Rubric
scope: For a subject-matter expert judging a deployed LearnPack course by taking it as a learner would, end to end. Twelve statements; each answered as agreement on the same five points. What it produces is the reference automated assessors are compared against — not a published verdict on a course, and not a score anyone reports.
evaluatorMaterials: the deployed course, all lessons, taken as a learner would take it

items.prompt: The course's objectives are phrased with observable action verbs.
items.guidance: Agree if every objective names an observable action a learner could be watched performing — solve, classify, build, debug. Disagree if objectives only list topics the course will cover, or name internal states you cannot observe from outside, such as 'understand', 'learn about' or 'get familiar with'.

items.prompt: The course starts at a point reachable from the audience's declared background.
items.guidance: Agree if what the course assumes you already know is either named for you or fair to assume of the audience it declares. Disagree if it demands knowledge that audience would not have, or leans on ideas it never names and that audience would not bring.

items.prompt: Every declared objective is developed by some part of the content.
items.guidance: Agree if every declared objective has a part of the content that actually develops it, not merely a mention. Disagree if any objective is only named in passing, with no part of the content actually developing it.

items.prompt: Each declared objective is measured by at least one of the assessment tasks the course offers.
items.guidance: Agree if every declared objective has a task that would show whether a learner can actually do it. Disagree if there are no tasks, if the tasks check something other than what the objectives declare, or if they only ask the learner to recall what was said.

items.prompt: New material is introduced through a problem, case or task that makes it needed, rather than starting from the explanation.
items.guidance: Agree if new material almost always arrives after a concrete problem or task that makes you want it. Disagree if lessons open with definitions and theory, and the reason to care — if it comes at all — comes afterwards.

items.prompt: When the course teaches how to do something, it shows it worked through step by step.
items.guidance: Agree if every skill the course teaches is shown being carried out before the learner is asked to do it. Disagree if the course describes how something is done without ever showing it done, or jumps from the description straight to the exercise.

items.prompt: The course connects new material to things the learner already knows.
items.guidance: Agree if new ideas are tied to prior knowledge, or to everyday experience this audience would have. Disagree if new ideas arrive with no bridge from anything the learner brings, as self-contained blocks of information.

items.prompt: Read in order, the course reads as one argument rather than a set of separate articles.
items.guidance: Agree if the course opens, develops and closes, and the order it uses is doing work — each part needs the ones before it. Disagree if the parts could be shuffled with little loss, because each stands on its own.

items.prompt: Later parts of the course put earlier parts to work instead of starting over.
items.guidance: Agree if later material consistently works with what came before, treating it as something the learner now has. Disagree if each part stands alone, and earlier material is explained again rather than used.

items.prompt: The course makes the connections between its lessons and ideas explicit, rather than leaving you to infer them.
items.guidance: This is not about whether the sequence is coherent, but about whether the course says so. Agree if the course tells you how its parts relate: why this comes after that, what an idea builds on. Disagree if lessons are presented one after another and you have to work out for yourself how they relate.

items.prompt: Ideas the course builds on are introduced before they are needed.
items.guidance: Agree if, where a lesson depends on an idea, that idea was introduced earlier in the course, or it is genuinely part of the background this course is written for. Disagree if lessons depend on ideas that were never introduced and that this audience would not be expected to bring.

items.prompt: The course grows more demanding at a pace someone arriving at it could follow.
items.guidance: Agree if the course gets steadily more demanding and each step is reachable from the one before. Disagree if it stays flat throughout, or if at least one lesson runs far ahead of the rest of the course.

frameworks.citation: Merrill, M. D. (2002). First Principles of Instruction. ETR&D, 50(3), 43-59.
Biggs, J. (1996). Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32, 347-364.
Anderson & Krathwohl (2001); Krathwohl (2002), Theory Into Practice, 41(4), 212-218.
Biggs & Collis (1982). Evaluating the Quality of Learning: The SOLO Taxonomy.
Schmidt, Wang & McKnight (2005); Schmidt, Houang & Cogan (2002). Curriculum coherence.
Duschl, Maeng & Sezen (2011). Learning progressions and teaching sequences.
